member_targets: The decision process or criteria musicians use in real time to select among competing intonation adjustments when harmonic, dynamic, thermal, and instrumental pressures conflict.

The decision process or criteria performers use in-performance to depart from the initial tuning reference — i.e., what cues or conditions (harmonic context, dynamics, temperature, ensemble blend) they monitor and how they judge that an intonation adjustment is warranted.
The physical mechanism by which temperature variation alters an instrument's pitch/intonation during performance.
The mechanism by which temperature changes and instrument behavior alter an instrument's pitch/intonation over the course of a performance, and the direction of those effects.
The physical/acoustic mechanism by which temperature changes and instrument behavior alter an instrument's sounding pitch after initial tuning, causing drift from the shared reference.
The mechanism and direction by which temperature change during performance alters an instrument's pitch/intonation, requiring players to adjust.
The decision criteria and cues performers use in-performance to judge when departing from the initial reference pitch in intonation is warranted.

The perceptual or judgmental criteria ensemble players use to determine that an intonation adjustment has achieved sufficient alignment — i.e., what cues or standards signal 'in tune enough' during tuning and performance.
The in-performance techniques and adjustment behaviors musicians use to correct pitch drift after the initial tuning reference, i.e., the ongoing methods of intonation correction during playing.
The decision criteria or basis performers use to select among competing locally-useful intonation adjustments in real time during performance.

An enumeration of the specific musical and physical influences arising during performance (e.g., harmonic context, dynamics, temperature, instrument behavior) that lead players to adjust intonation away from the initially agreed reference tuning.
The decision criterion or basis performers use to select among several equally locally useful intonation adjustments in a given moment.

The mechanisms or practices by which ensemble players sustain accurate intonation during performance once the initial reference tone has ceased sounding — i.e., what they rely on and adjust to in place of the audible anchor.
The specific in-performance techniques and adjustment behaviors players use to correct pitch drift caused by changing physical conditions such as temperature.

The real-time mechanisms and processes by which performers modify pitch during playing to accommodate shifting harmonic contexts — i.e., how the adjustment is accomplished (perceptual feedback, technique, coordination), not merely that intonation varies.

The in-performance techniques and coordination processes by which ensemble players continuously adjust and reconcile intonation as harmonic and other contextual demands pull pitches away from the initial shared reference.
The perceptual criterion or cue players use to judge that their pitch is sufficiently aligned with the reference — i.e., what signals 'close enough' during tuning.

The ongoing mechanisms and practices by which ensemble players keep intonation aligned during performance despite differing rates of instrument drift, i.e., how continuous adjustment is coordinated after the initial reference tuning.
The ongoing mechanisms or practices by which ensemble players keep pitches aligned during performance despite divergent per-instrument tendencies, rather than the initial tuning procedure.
